Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Ravi was 36, a South Asian man who had grown up in an apartment in a dense, noisy part of the city and now lived alone in a quieter complex after his divorce. He worked as an accountant, a job that suited his preference for routine, predictable hours, and spaces where numbers made more sense than people. His parents had separated long ago, but what stayed with him was not the separation itself so much as the years before it, when he repeatedly witnessed his father assaulting his mother in their home. He could still picture the narrow hallway outside the kitchen, the orange light over the stove, and the sound of his mother crying out while he stood frozen at a distance, too young to intervene and too frightened to move. Even now, he could not describe those scenes fluently; when he tried, the details seemed to catch in his throat, as if the events existed more as a surge of terror than as a story he could tell. He would sometimes say only, “I was there,” and stop there, because putting it into words felt impossible.

In the years after those episodes, Ravi noticed that certain moments could throw him straight back into the same helpless state. A loud argument in the apartment above him, a sudden thud from a neighboring unit, or the sharp sound of a man’s voice rising in anger could bring on an instant rush of the old fear. When that happened, his body reacted before he could think: his heart pounded, his shoulders tightened, and he felt a jolt through his chest and stomach that made him want to get away immediately. He described living with a body that was “always on,” as though he had to stay ready for something bad to happen. At work he kept himself in a constant scan of the office, noticing every slammed drawer, every raised voice from the break room, every abrupt movement behind him. He sat near the door when he could, not because he liked the view but because he felt safer having an exit. Colleagues knew him as careful and efficient, but they also noticed that he seemed tense, difficult to startle but easy to unsettle, as if his whole frame were braced for impact.

The memory itself came back in a way that felt less like remembering and more like being thrown back into the event. Certain cues could do it without warning. A man shouting in the street below his apartment, the impact of a book dropped onto a desk, or even a television scene with a heated domestic argument could make the old images surge in full force. In those moments Ravi was not simply reminded of what he had seen; he felt the same terror he had felt as a boy standing helplessly in the hallway. The fear was immediate and physical, and he often had to step outside, grip the railing of the fire escape, or sit in his car until his breathing settled. He hated how little control he had over these episodes. What troubled him most was that they arrived uninvited, as if the past could break into any ordinary day.

Over time, Ravi had come to hold a bleak view of what had happened and of his own life. He spoke with visible bitterness about the fact that the people responsible had faced no consequences. His father had gone on with his life, and his mother had done what she could to survive, but there had never been any accountability for the violence Ravi witnessed as a child. That absence sat heavily with him. He had expected, at some point, that someone would acknowledge what had been done, but instead he learned to carry the injustice alone. He also described himself now as a different person from the boy he had once been, saying that he used to be happy and that now he felt miserable most of the time. The contrast was painful to him because he remembered being lighter, more open, and less guarded before those years in the apartment changed the way he saw people and the world. He had come to believe that bad things could happen to him no matter how carefully he behaved, and that belief showed itself in his daily life in the way he watched for danger even in ordinary settings.

After his divorce, Ravi became even more isolated, spending evenings in his apartment with the television low and the curtains drawn. His work remained stable, but he noticed that he was increasingly strained by the ordinary unpredictability of office life and by the ways family obligations sometimes brought him into crowded, emotionally charged settings. He found himself making excuses to leave gatherings early, especially if there was raised speech or tension in the room. Recently, a heated exchange near his desk at work triggered a violent surge of physical fear so strong that he had to lock himself in a restroom until it passed. That episode frightened him not only because of how intense it was, but because he realized how little confidence he had that things would ever feel different. He sought help now because he was tired of living as though danger were always about to arrive, and because he no longer wanted his world to keep shrinking around old memories he could not shut off. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was some way to feel less trapped by the past and less certain that the same bad things would keep happening to him.
